paras: The attempted lynching of Joe Deberry was a series of mob attempts in southern Illinois between July 30 and August 30, 1915, to seize and hang Deberry, a Black servant accused of murdering Mrs. James H. Martin, a Murphysboro lawyer's wife. Officers kept him from mobs at Murphysboro, Marion and Harrisburg, and militia guarded his trial, where he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to hang. Southern papers cited the case to answer the Chicago Tribune's criticism of lynching in the South.

Mrs. Martin, 45, was beaten to death in her Murphysboro home on the afternoon of Friday, July 30, and was found dying by her sister and daughter. Deberry, her servant, paroled through her efforts months earlier, was arrested within hours.

That evening, as a mob of some 500 men formed near the jail, the sheriff "spirited the prisoner away" by automobile. A Kentucky weekly said the mob "stormed the jail" as Sheriff James A. White sped for Marion, where ringleaders in twelve automobiles raised another mob. The Cape Girardeau weekly reported that crowds at Marion and Harrisburg each announced they would hang him. Accounts of the route differ, some placing him at Harrisburg and others at the Mound City jail by way of Harrisburg or Carmi.

By July 31 he was in the Harrisburg jail, guarded against a new mob reported forming nearby, and a coroner's jury held him for the murder. After officers announced on August 2 that he had confessed to Sheriff White and Sheriff George W. Russell of Saline County, men in Murphysboro talked openly of a mob to go to Harrisburg.

Judge D. T. Hartwell set a special court term for August 30 and asked for troops, and three companies of the Fourth Infantry were ordered out. On the night of August 29 a mob of several hundred surrounded the Harrisburg jail and demanded Deberry. Taken out by a ruse, he was brought by special train under military escort to Murphysboro, where a crowd of a hundred offered only "mutterings of lynching".

On August 30 Deberry was indicted, pleaded guilty and was sentenced to hang on October 16, all in less than six hours. The AP credited the militia with preventing violence amid "murmurings of possible mob violence", and the East St. Louis Daily Journal reported that hundreds "cheered repeatedly" at the sentence. Mrs. Martin's husband reportedly died of shock, and her son asked to spring the trap; no arrest of any mob member was reported.

The first wire story was headlined as a murder ("Woman Hacked to Death") and mentioned the mob only in its last sentence. Regional papers soon made the chase the story, with headlines such as "Officer Eludes Mobs" in East St. Louis and "Sheriff Flees From 3 Lynching Parties" in Cape Girardeau. White papers called Deberry "the negro", later "the confessed negro murderer", and trial headlines such as "Negro Slayer Sent to Rope" stressed speed.

Southern papers turned the case against the North, starting with the Monroe Journal's headline "Tried it In Illinois". The Richmond Times-Dispatch told the Chicago Tribune that a Murphysboro prisoner had to be removed by militia "to escape the wrath of the mob". A Columbia Record editorial reprinted in South Carolina recalled the Tribune's attacks over the Leo M. Frank lynching and mocked Illinois for guarding "a gentleman of color from the dear citizens of Illinois". The Fayette Falcon of Tennessee said the Harrisburg mob showed "human nature is just the same north or south".

Black papers covered the case briefly and without editorial comment on the mobs. The Metropolis Weekly Gazette ran the wire confession story under "Lyghing Spirit Is Fired Anew", and the Denver Star headed its siege item "Sheriff Outwits Mob". The Indianapolis Freeman's Mound City correspondent wrote that the crime had inflamed race prejudice, praised efforts "to let the law take its course", and advised: "Silence is golden for us at this time."

Early reports named a hatchet or ax as the weapon, while the confession reported by officers and Deberry's court statement named a poker. The stated motive shifted from robbery, to a grudge, to anger at being asked if he was drunk, to her refusal of 50 cents, each version from officers, unnamed sources or Deberry in custody.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Joe Deberry
bases: Mobs at Murphysboro, Marion and Harrisburg pursued, stormed jails and announced they would hang Deberry, a prisoner accused of murder, but officers kept him from them and no one was killed (A11, A14, A22).

Crowds of hundreds sought to hang Deberry without lawful authority in reprisal for the murder of Mrs. Martin (A1, A14, A22), but every attempt failed and he was tried and sentenced in court (A25), so this was an attempted lynching, not a lynching.
Independent wire, regional and Black-press reports agree that mobs formed at Murphysboro and in the towns he was taken to and that officers moved him to avoid them (A1, A4, A11, A14, A22, A34).

accounts.label: Wire report (first day)
accounts.gist: Mrs. Martin was hacked to death with a hatchet; Deberry was arrested and, as a mob of 500 formed near the jail, the sheriff spirited him away.

accounts.label: Regional accounts of the chase
accounts.gist: Mobs followed or formed ahead of the sheriff at Marion and Harrisburg and announced they would hang Deberry; the sheriff eluded them and lodged him at Mound City or Harrisburg.

accounts.label: Officers' account of a confession
accounts.gist: Officers said Deberry confessed at Harrisburg to killing Mrs. Martin with a poker after she asked if he was drunk; the confession comes only from officers.

accounts.label: Courtroom statement
accounts.gist: At trial Deberry pleaded guilty and said he killed her because she refused him 50 cents.

accounts.label: Black correspondent at Mound City
accounts.gist: The crime had inflamed race prejudice in southern Illinois and hurt law-abiding Black residents; local leaders were working to let the law take its course.

framing.detail: First reports headlined the killing ('Woman Hacked to Death', 'Woman Beaten and Chopped to Death') and mentioned the mob only in the final sentence.
Follow-ups made the flight the story ('Officer Eludes Mobs', 'Sheriff Flees From 3 Lynching Parties') without condemning the mobs.
A Kentucky weekly ran 'Woman Is Slain by Negro Axman' under the same headline as the Temple, Texas, burning and stated Deberry's guilt as fact before any trial.
Trial stories stressed speed and punishment ('Negro Slayer Sent to Rope', 'Court and Jury Convict Negro in Record Time') and credited the militia with preventing violence.

Southern editorials ('Tried it In Illinois') used the Illinois mobs to answer the Chicago Tribune's criticism of Southern lynching, mocking Illinois rather than condemning the mobs; one said it showed 'human nature is just the same north or south'.
The Metropolis Weekly Gazette ran the wire confession story under 'Negro Admits He Murdered Lawyer's Wife' and 'Lyghing Spirit Is Fired Anew'.
The Freeman's Mound City correspondent called the crime brutal, regretted the race prejudice it stirred, backed letting the law take its course and counseled silence.
The Denver Star ('Sheriff Outwits Mob') and St. Louis Argus ran brief news items, the Star calling Deberry 'a colored man'.
